Senses.Explanation: To overturn completely, down to the bottom. Masters use the strong verb for a decisive change in how someone faces a question or inherited form; the surrounding talk still tests whether the change is real. At a transmission ceremony Konggu Daocheng says his disciples have overturned things so completely that he must lay out the source stream before them. Yanju Deshen gives the phrase as a direct answer to a monk who asks what to do when neither a blow nor a needle can penetrate. Yingshan Zhiyin says that only someone fully overturned can handle both teaching and encounter without leaning on a borrowed explanation. Juelang Daosheng urges listeners to break out of their own old nest and overturn another's inherited den, taking up a staff even against buddhas and ancestors. Minshu Ruxiang makes complete overturning part of a verse after a question about sage and ordinary person, before saying the Buddha-seed grows by conditions. Tianyin Yuanxiu tells retreatants to overturn what he has just described and checks whether seclusion hides continued attachment. Yingning Zhijing calls for a forceful overturning after urging students to give up old tricks, then continues with the old tree-and-vine case. Neishao Zhizhong says a clean teaching threshold requires overturning completely before striking his staff and warning the assembly to distinguish what is clear from what is confused.

Senses.Note: Verbal and noun-like grammar denotes the same event/state and does not warrant a split. The related term “interpretive awakening” (解悟) is a text-drawn contrast, not an annotator’s ranking.

Senses.Explanation: Wuyi Yuanlai supplies the clearest corpus definition: there are two awakenings, “interpretive awakening obtained from written words and speech” and “thorough awakening obtained by investigating on one’s own part”; he adds, “interpretive awakening is like hearing someone describe a thing; thorough awakening is like seeing the thing with one’s own eyes” (解悟者如聞人說物，徹悟者如親眼見物). Other records say not to stop if one has not thoroughly awakened, describe the World-honored One seeing the morning star and thoroughly awakening, and contrast the many who thoroughly awaken with the equally many who misunderstand. Thus the Chan record bends an ordinary intensive verb into a named contrast with “interpretive awakening” (解悟), while also using it in lineage biographies; the direct contrast, not an imported theory of enlightenment, controls the gloss.

Entries.SourceTerm: 方便遣情猶不是，更除方便太無端

Senses.PreferredTarget: Even using expedients to dispel attachment is not right; abolishing expedients altogether is far too unwarranted.
SearchAliases: even using expedients to dispel attachment is not right; abolishing expedients altogether is far too unwarranted.
Senses.Note: Attachment translates the compressed qing in the local setting of feelings, ties and claims. The pair neither approves every expedient nor commands a mechanical withdrawal; each retirement gives it a different present force.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師初受訥讓，住圓通時，年始二十八。自以前輩讓善叢林，責己甚重，故敬嚴臨眾，以公滅私。於是宗風大振。未幾，訥厭閒寂。郡守至，自陳客情。大守惻然目師，師笑唯唯而已。明日陞座曰：昔法眼有偈曰：難難難是遣情難，情盡圓明一顆寒。方便遣情猶不是，更除方便太無端。大眾且道情作麼生遣？喝一喝，下座，負包而去。一眾大驚，挽之不可。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X82/X82n1571.xml). Complete Five Lamps (Vols. 34–120). Baiyun Shouduan takes over Yuantong after its former abbot, Ne, yields the post. Ne later becomes unhappy in retirement and tells the prefect about his circumstances. The prefect looks sympathetically toward Baiyun, who merely smiles assent. The following day Baiyun ascends the seat and explicitly raises a verse attributed to Fayan Wenyi: dispelling attachment is difficult; even using expedients to dispel it is not right, yet abolishing expedients is too unwarranted. How is attachment to be dispelled? Baiyun asks, then shouts, descends, shoulders his pack and leaves despite the assembly's attempts to keep him. Fayan supplies the quoted verse voice; Baiyun makes it a present question answered by relinquishing his office. The narrative does not say that every departure or every act of yielding would have the same force.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉：「白雲端祖遊廬山，圓通訥讓以院事。不久，太守來，通敘以東堂之苦，太守以目顧端，端低頭。至明日上堂，舉法眼偈云：『難難難是遣情難，一顆圓明透水寒。方便遣情猶不是，更除方便太無端。』喝一喝下座，腰包而去，眾挽之不可。山僧今日因有一頌：遣情退院事方閒，破院驅馳未足觀。從此清風遍寰宇，圓明千古逼人寒。且道普明今日解散又作麼生？啼得血流無用處，不如緘口過殘年。」喝一喝下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB424.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xiangyan. At Puming, Xiangyan addresses the assembly when the retreat and ordination period end and he is taking leave. After distinguishing original freedom from the practical need for sustained discipline, he raises Baiyun's retirement and its explicitly attributed Fayan verse. Xiangyan adds his own poem: retiring to dispel attachment leaves affairs quiet; rushing about a broken-down monastery is not enough to behold; from here a pure breeze spreads throughout the world and rounded clarity chills through the ages. He then asks what his own dispersal from Puming amounts to, closing with the image of a cuckoo crying until blood flows in vain and choosing to keep silent for the remaining years. He shouts and descends. The exact pair remains Fayan's old verse within Baiyun's quoted use, while Xiangyan tests it against his own present departure. His new poem and final image should not be flattened into simple imitation or a general rule to abandon responsibility.

Occurrences.Kwic: 退院，上堂。在昔白雲端祖住圓通退院，上堂曰：難難難是遣情難，情盡圓明一顆寒，方便遣情猶不是，更除方便太無端。大眾！且情又如何遣聻？遂一喝，下座。拽杖出山，清風古韻，仰止千秋。今日不肖遠孫乍主雪竇，況味相侔，用拈一偈以續貂後：秉命住持九越月，艱危奚止一絲懸？翠峰法叔親臨到，撾鼓陞堂告脫肩。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X82/X82n1571.xml). Complete Five Lamps (Vols. 34–120). Xuedou's Yi'an Yuan opens his retirement address by recalling Baiyun leaving Yuantong, quoting the same verse pair and question about dispelling attachment before describing Baiyun's shout and departure. He calls that an ancient pure style worthy of lasting respect, but says his own circumstances resemble it only as an unworthy distant descendant. His new verse specifies nine months in office, dangers hanging by less than a thread, and the arrival of his lineage uncle Cuifeng to take the drum, ascend the hall and release him from the burden. The pair is thus reused within a distinct handover of responsibility rather than another copy of Baiyun's original event. Fayan remains the attributed earlier verse speaker; Yi'an Yuan is the present retiring teacher. The lamp supplies his source name, but no canonical personal identity is forced beyond that evidence.

Senses.Explanation: The couplet places a west-flowing river sound where even Yu’s power does not reach. Yan’an closes a hall question with it; Shanduo Zhenzai gives it after calling for recognition of one’s own nose; Longyin Yushan Rui uses it after asking whether the assembly understands; Shending Yikui leans on his staff and gives it as the requested line.
